content.title: Thanks for your feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to review our manuscript and provide your feedback. We provide some clarifications below. 

> Algorithm 1 is not clear: train what model? The entire model in steps 1-3 in Figure 2?

Yes, exactly.

> Step 1 of Figure 2 is not clear to me: Are the costs measured for various configurations of a solver or are the configurations fixed for all runs?

The costs measured are using a fixed configuration for all runs (the default solver configuration).
These costs are used to define similarity as in Step 1. So, costs here are measured for a fixed configuration. The various configurations are obtained offline using SMAC, and not used during training. They are only used during inference time (next clarifying question below).

> It’s not clear to me where the solver configurations for Algorithm 2 step 4 come from.

We use SMAC to perform a configuration space search on the training instances. There have been over 51,000 unique configurations explored. They are stored in a database that can be queried during inference (Appendix E). The methodology section discusses details under _Configuration Space Exploration_. In addition, the experiments section (_Comparing to Baselines_) reports numbers of unique configurations.

> Figure 5 is not clear to me. Which baseline is shown in the figure?

It is the baseline with the lowest cost on a given instance amongst: (1) default SCIP Config, (2) SMAC, (3) Hydra-MIP and (4) Shallow Embedding + KNN.

We are updating the manuscript to include the recommended clarifications.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Existing general Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solvers have up to thousands of various configuration parameters affecting the solver's performance and solution's quality. Searching for a good set of parameters is expensive, or infeasible. The paper presents a weakly supervised metric learning model *MILPTune* for predicting suitable configurations. MILP instances are represented as bipartite graphs and the architecture consists of GNN based embedding trained with a triplet loss. Triplets of MILP instances are pre-processed so that positive/negative pairs have small/large solution's cost (primal bound with default conf. parameters) difference. On inference time, a MILP instance is embedded and a nearest neighbour's configuration (found by an existing offline search methods) is selected. Experiments on ML4CO datasets with SCIP solver show that MILPTune predicts configuration parameters with a lower primal bound. The model assumes that all the instances are from the same distribution (coming from the same combinatorial problem).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
- Original idea of using metric learning to reuse known good parameter configurations for similar instances.
- The model is simple and the scheme is quite straightforward. The ability of the MILP instance embedding to predict a primal bound obtained from default configuration is experimentally tested against competing methods.
- Mostly easy to read and understand the overall idea.
- The paper contributes to a problem that is well-known, hard and unsolved satisfactorily.

## Weaknesses
**Evaluation** 
- The comparison (Table 1) uses weird relative-improvement metric ('solution’s cost improvement over the lowest cost from other methods’ configurations') and the achieved costs are not presented. The probem with this metric is that it highly depends on the performance of others and **ignores** the cases when the evaluated method is not winning. Consider this example with methods A, B, C and two equaly-sized sets of instances $I_1$ and $I_2$ (see the table below). Method A always achieves cost 100 and never wins (Impr=0), B wins narrowely (99) on $I_2$ which makes the improvement around 1%, C wins by a margin on $I_1$ but looses terribly on $I_2$ and still gains Improvement 50%.  However, all methods achieve on average the same costs (only std differs) but C has 50 times higher improvement!
- The design relies on the fact that instances that have similar primal bound with the default configuration will have similar (lower) primal bound when the solver is run with another (better) set of conf. parameters. This is not evident and it is not explained, quoted or tested. Results of Fig 4. may tell us something, but it also contains information about the embedding and nearest neighbour search.
- I do not agree that Fig. 4a shows any correlation. No statistics is provided (eg. correlation coefficient) and MAE is not relevant here. (4b shows clear correlation)
- Fig. 5 also does not contain any information about costs, only abou the winning method.
- NeurIPS competition [ML4CO] 'Configuration task' uses a 'primal-dual integral' as a metric. The authors claim (Appendix B) that 'primal bound proved to be a more robust metric' because using primal-dual integral 'has yielded difficulties in finding a threshold...' This is not a valid argument; it rather suggests that the method is brittle and positive results were cherry-picked.
- Therefore, I am not convinced that the performance of MILPTune supports the authors' claims unless they provide more solid statistics.

| Method | costs on $I_1$ | costs on $I_2$ | Avg | Impr. |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| A | 100 | 100 | 100 | 0 |

| B | 101 | 99 | 100 | ~1% |

| C | 50 | 150 | 100 | 50% |

**presentation**
- Some parts of the metric learning description is confusing. I don't understand what the paragraph with '...Euclidean distance is less meaningful in higher dimensions...' is trying to say. Next, there is no distance function $d$. Only the (learned) embedding $f$ to some Euclidean space is used.
- Description of baselines Hydra-MIP and its Shallow Embedding is very vague.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper uses known components for metric learning in the area of MILP configuration which is novel. The setup description is more or less clear, the code with instructions are supplemented and it should not be a problem with running it. The evaluation quality is low and not convincing.

The paper contributes to a hard and important problem, but there are gaps and concerns in the methods evaluation.

My evaluation is biased since I already reviewed this paper earlier. The paper did not change singnificantly and did not fully address all the objections that led to rejection. My review is also similar.

content.title: Thanks for the feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for agreeing to reconsider our manuscript for review, and for the detailed feedback. We provide some clarifications below. 

> The comparison (Table 1) uses weird relative-improvement metric ('solution’s cost improvement over the lowest cost from other methods’ configurations') and the achieved costs are not presented.

In fact, the relative-improvement metric was one of the suggestions of the previous reviews. Previously, we only tracked “Wins”, and did not measure improvements, but they were included this time.

> Consider this example with methods A, B, C

This is why we consider the number of “Wins”. The idea is that when we say method A is better than method C, we don’t just want to know how many instances it solved with a lower cost (and won), but also how much “lower” cost it was compared to the second-best baseline. Figure 5 complements this view by showing why a baseline method performed better than our proposed method. It shows that the nearest neighbor found was in fact not very close in distance (i.e. > $\alpha$).

> This is not a valid argument; it rather suggests that the method is brittle and positive results were cherry-picked.

As discussed in the methodology section, pooling anchor-positives and anchor-negatives depends on the subjective definition of similarity. Defining similarity based on primal-dual integral did not work, and this fact was included in the manuscript for full transparency. The reason it did not work is that solving the same instance in two separate solver runs using the same configuration parameters, machine, environment, seeds and time limit **results in different primal-dual integral** depending on the granularity of timesteps the solver was queried (in order to calculate the area under the curve). This breaks the subjective definition of similarity because if the “exact” instance (not “similar”) is not actually similar in two different solver runs.

> The paper did not change singnificantly and did not fully address all the objections that led to rejection. My review is also similar.

In fact, the whole experimental section was re-evaluated and all results and visualizations are based on new findings and results.

content.title: Response to the authors
content.comment:
Thank you for your replies.

The previous reviews are not public, so l do not want to mention or quote specific objections raised and discussed before. My current rating was also not based on past complaints; I added information about my previous experience with this paper to explain to the authors why some parts of my review are similar.

I appreciate that some qualitative comparison was added, and we can see 'how much' a method wins among others. However, we must also see 'how much' it loses in the remaining cases. The reported metric should serve as a reasonable guideline for practitioners to select the best method (from A, B, and C in my simplified example). When we stick to one method, we will deal with all outcomes (and not only the winning ones), and we need to know what results we can expect. From the relative improvement metric, one can have unrealistic expectations about method C, but on average, all A, B, and C perform the same.

I'm afraid I still have to disagree that Fig. 4a shows any correlation. And I still do not understand why 'The Euclidean distance is less meaningful in higher dimensions...'.

I want to encourage the authors to take as much as possible from the feedback given by all the reviews to revise the paper thoroughly. I believe it contains an interesting contribution to predicting solver configurations.

I still vote for rejection at this stage, primarily because of the weak evaluation.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a method for algorithm parameter tuning in mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solvers. The method uses a graph neural network to embed an input MILP instance into a latent space, then applies nearest neighbor to predict well-performing parameter settings from nearby solved instances.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is confusingly written and light on details on how the method integrates with the end application (tuning MILP solvers for greater computational performance).

Clarity:
The paper is confusingly written, particularly Section 4. After reading I do not have a clear sense of how the algorithm parameters (what is being tuned by the method) fit into the picture. For example: how do you get parameter configuration diversity? Algorithm 2 is meant to produce a candidate configuration associated with "nearby" previously observed MILP instances, but the important detail of _how_ those "nearest neighbors stored configs" are determined or set is not discussed. The only explicit mention I can find is in Section 5 where you state: "Given the training dataset, we run the MILP solver on all instances using the default parameters configuration of the solver". If so, how is diversity introduced? Internally by the solver dynamically determining what "default" means? Or externally according to some form of randomness introduced by the authors? 

See also the following section of the review for more specific points in the paper that could benefit from greater clarity.

MILP solver performance:
 The paper does not make sufficiently clear the way in which they are using a MILP solver: attempting to find the best feasible solution within a fixed time budget. This is a reasonable use, but needs to be highlighted early and explicitly. For example, the abstract says that "using the default solver configuration leads to poor suboptimal solutions". This is only the case when the user imposes a hard time limit: with sufficient time, the solver should always converge to an optimal solution if one exists (modulo e.g. numerical issues). This decision colors the story told by Figure 1 (see below).

Assuming that instances with varying parameter settings are being considered, the paper would benefit greatly from an investigation of _how_ the suggested parameters differ. How diverse are the sets of parameters that are learned? Is it the case that a small number of parameters (e.g., high-level "emphasis" parameters) are the main drivers of the relative performance? Etc.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Figure 1 is framed confusingly. Really what you are measuring here is the progress of the solver within a fixed time window (I believe this is what "T" is, though the author's do not state this explicitly). This is a reasonable thing to measure as motivation, but please explicitly state and justify these choices (of the exeriment, of time limit, and of the metric used to measure solver performance) in the text.
* Algorithm 1 is vague on important details: how is the anchor selected in 1? What if no such p exists in 2? What does "much greater than" mean in practice? Etc.
* In Table 1: What does "Wins" track? Is "Imprv." absolute improvement in the objective value, or a percentage improvement? The most meaningful number to report here would be percentage improvement w.r.t. the best known dual bound for the instance. What is the "No Solution Found" configuration?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has major weaknesses in the clarity of the presentation, and overall the connection with the underlying application (MILP solvers) is lacking important details and discussion. As a result, I am unable to fully assess the quality of the contributions.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Thanks for the feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for your feedback. We provide some clarifications below. 

> For example: how do you get parameter configuration diversity?

We use SMAC to get parameter configuration diversity. The total number of unique configurations explored were over 51,000. Details are presented in the methodology section under **Configuration Space Exploration.** and revisited in the experiments section in **Comparing to Baselines**. 

> but the important detail of how those "nearest neighbors stored configs" are determined or set is not discussed.

Nearest neighbors are determined using KNN on the learned embedding of the problem instances and the new unseen instance (described in Algorithm 2). Further details on data management and how nearest neighbors are retrieved is discussed in Appendix E.

> with sufficient time, the solver should always converge to an optimal solution if one exists

The problems presented in the datasets are NP-Hard. With large instance sizes, it takes exponential time to solve to optimality. In face, in some instances, even letting the solver run forever would not yield an optimal solution if the problem is infeasible (because of the constraints). Therefore, in a real-world setting, a time limit is always imposed on the solver, especially in applications where real-time decision making is needed (e.g. optimizing VM placements in datacenters)

> how the suggested parameters differ. How diverse are the sets of parameters that are learned?

Our method does not learn sets of parameters. Our method learns embeddings of problem instances that are close to each other (euclidean distance) if the costs of these instances are similar under the same parameters configuration. Using the learned embeddings, a new unseen problem instance can be mapped to the learned embedding space and a parameters configuration can be predicted from the nearest neighbor instance.

As for the diversity of the parameters themselves, our data store includes over 51,000 unique parameter configurations that were explored offline using SMAC.

> Algorithm 1 is vague on important details: how is the anchor selected in 1? What if no such p exists in 2? 

The methodology section under **1. MILP Triplet Sampling.** offers the details for Algorithm 1. The anchor is any instance in the training dataset and a positive instance is any instance in the same training dataset that has a solution cost under a threshold $C_{thr}$ when it was solved using the same configuration. There is always such $p$ since  the training procedure controls the mining step from the training dataset.

> What does "much greater than" mean in practice?

It means that the cost difference between instances $I_i$ and $I_j$ is larger than the threshold $C_{thr}$ by at least 2x.

> What does "Wins" track?  

Wins track the number of instances in the validation dataset that a given method offered a parameters configuration that resulted in a lower-cost solution. The method that “wins” is the method that offers a parameters configuration that resulted in the lowest-cost solution among other methods.

> What is the "No Solution Found" configuration?

In some instances in the validation dataset, the solver was not able to find a feasible solution within the time limit under the given parameters configuration by the respective method. These are called "No Solution Found".

We are updating the manuscript to include your recommended clarifications.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a machine learning-based approach to configure MILP solvers. Specifically, a metric learning model based on a graph neural network is trained to learn a distance space that encodes the similarity of MILP instances. Given an unseen instance, KNN is used to predict the best parameters configuration based on the learned distance space.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: Configuring MILP solvers is an interesting and significant research question, and using machine learning to select parameters is a promising approach. However, there has been a lot of work in meta-learning and algorithm selection that uses machine learning to configure algorithms/methods. In this sense, the idea of this paper is not new. Using deep metric learning to learn a distance between MILP instances is an interesting idea. However, it still lacks novelty as it simply applies an existing technique to the MILP problem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written and easy to follow. It contains sufficient details to reproduce the results and the source code is available. 
The paper lacks novelty as discussed above. In addition, a lot of existing work in algorithm/parameter selection and meta-learning is not discussed in this paper.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper724 by Reviewer 4jGx

content.title: Thank you for the feedback
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to review our manuscript and provide your feedback. We believe that our method advances the state-of-the-art in configuring the hyper-parameters of MILP solvers, and offers a novel view of using an unsupervised learning method (i.e. metric learning) in addressing an important problem. It shows the potential of metric learning in the hyper-parameter tuning line of research.  

We provide some clarifications below. 

> 1. How was alpha chosen?

$\alpha$ is a small value that controls the desired difference between the anchor-positive distance and the anchor-negative distance. Setting it too high results in the model overfitting the training data for learning the deep embeddings. Setting it too low could lead to the $d_{ap}$ canceling $d_{an}$ and the model stops learning. In our experiments, we set it to `0.1` based on the embeddings of the datasets under experiments.

> 2. How was the parameters of GNN set?

The parameters were set as _in Valentin et. al., Instance-wise algorithm configuration with graph neural networks, 2022_.

> 3. Was the model trained separately for each of three problems? How does it work if a single model is trained across all the three problems?

Yes. The model was trained separately for each of the three problems. As mentioned in the limitation subsection, our method relies on data coming from the same distribution. The reason is that pooling for anchor-positives and anchor-negatives is based on the instances’ costs, and similarity is defined by assigning instances to buckets that divide that range of costs of that specific problem distribution. Using instances from different problems is limited by the definition of similarity, since the range of the expected costs is different from one problem to the other.

> 4. It seems that the deep metric embedding method does not improve the shallow embedding 
significantly according to the experimental results.

In Table 1, we show that in the instances that it improves, the cost reduction is 10% to 67%. In the instances it does not improve their costs, we show, in Figure 5, that it was because the nearest neighbor to the validation instance had an embedding that is not close enough to any of the training instances in the learned embedding space, while our method excels when it finds a nearest neighbor that is close (<0.2) to the validation instance embedding.
